whatYouSee: A thick shell of calcium wraps around one whole lung and that side of the chest has shrunk.
whyItMatters: Old pleural infection such as tuberculous empyema can leave a thick calcified peel that traps the lung. This restricts breathing on that side.

condition.igTitle: THE LUNG IN A STONE SHELL
requiredObservations: a thick continuous rind of dense calcification wrapping around the outer surface of the left lung like a shell with a shrunken left hemithorax and crowded left ribs while the right lung is normal
The visible anatomy matches the requested PA chest and the declared age and anatomical exceptions.

defects: Unexplained additional image findings: ["Large left-sided pneumothorax with visible visceral pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings — not consistent with calcified fibrothorax, which would show a dense calcified pleural rind encasing a shrunken lung","No calcification whatsoever is visible along the left pleural surface or wrapping the left lung","The left hemithorax is not shrunken and the left ribs are not crowded — findings are opposite to what fibrothorax produces","The collapsed/retracted left lung opacity is consistent with compressive atelectasis from pneumothorax, not fibrothorax entrapment"]

findings: Right lung: normal aeration, normal bronchovascular markings, no focal consolidation, no pleural effusion, right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle well defined

Left lung: large left-sided pneumothorax occupying the lateral two-thirds of the left hemithorax with a visible visceral pleural line; the collapsed left lung is retracted toward the left hilum and appears opacified/atelectatic; lung markings absent peripheral to the pleural line
Mediastinum: trachea appears midline or only minimally deviated to the right; cardiac silhouette not appreciably shifted, suggesting no significant tension physiology at this moment
No obvious rib fractures identified on visible bony structures
Left shoulder region appears intact; right shoulder included at image margin
differential: Large spontaneous left-sided pneumothorax (primary or secondary)
Traumatic left-sided pneumothorax with associated lung collapse
Tension pneumothorax (early or partial; cannot exclude given size, though mediastinal shift is minimal)
anatomyConcerns: The mediastinum does not show the marked contralateral shift expected with a true tension pneumothorax, but pneumothorax size is very large — close clinical and hemodynamic correlation is essential
Left lower zone opacity likely represents compressive atelectasis of the collapsed lung rather than independent parenchymal disease; cannot fully exclude underlying consolidation
Slight rotation of the patient may be present, which could affect assessment of mediastinal position
